title: CSS foundations
summary: Connect a stylesheet, target an element, and inspect the result.
points: HTML describes meaning; CSS changes presentation. Keep headings, labels, and links meaningful.
Link an external stylesheet from the document head with rel="stylesheet" and the correct href.
A rule pairs a selector with declarations inside braces. Each declaration has a property, a colon, and a value.
A class selector starts with a dot; the HTML class attribute contains the name without the dot.
Check the Network panel for missing stylesheets and the Styles panel for invalid declarations.
code:
<!-- In the document head -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">

/* In styles.css */
.card {
  color: #263238;
  background-color: #fff5fa;
  padding: 1rem;
}
output: An element with class="card" receives the text color, background, and inner spacing. The link must point to the saved CSS file.
mistake: Writing .card in the HTML class attribute creates the wrong class name. Use class="card".
challenge: Add styles.css to your HTML planner. Style one heading and one card, then deliberately break and repair the stylesheet path.

title: Selectors & cascade
summary: Understand why a declaration wins before adding another override.
points: The cascade considers origin, importance, layers, specificity, and ordering. Specificity is only part of that process.
Within the same origin, importance, and layer, an ID selector is more specific than a class, which is more specific than an element selector.
When competing declarations otherwise tie, the later declaration wins. HTML class order does not decide this.
Some properties such as color inherit; margins do not normally inherit. A declaration on the child can replace an inherited value.
Use small class selectors and inspect crossed-out declarations. Avoid scattering !important to hide a misunderstanding.

rows: Some values flow from parent to child

output: The class selector beats the element selector despite appearing earlier. This comparison assumes equal origin, importance, and cascade layer.
mistake: “The last rule always wins” ignores earlier cascade steps. A higher-specificity rule can beat a later weaker selector.
challenge: Inspect a planner paragraph with two competing color rules. Explain which rule wins, then remove the unnecessary override.

diagram.title: Selectors & cascade
diagram.caption: Understand why a declaration wins before adding another override.

title: Box model & sizing
summary: Make space predictable from content through the outer margin.
points: The box model has content, padding, border, and margin. Padding is inside the border; margin separates boxes.
With content-box, a declared width excludes padding and borders. With border-box, that width includes them.
Use max-width with a flexible width to constrain reading areas without forcing horizontal overflow.
Set min-width: 0 when a flex or grid item needs to shrink below its automatic minimum. Long text may also need wrapping.
Adjacent vertical block margins can collapse in normal flow; margins in flex and grid layouts do not collapse with each other.
output: The planner never requests a width larger than its containing block. Padding is included in that width, and the card can wrap long content.
mistake: Adding a large fixed width to a card can overflow a phone even if its text size looks reasonable.
challenge: Inspect one card in the box-model panel. Compare its size under content-box and border-box, and fix overflow at 320px.

diagram.title: Box model & sizing
diagram.caption: Make space predictable from content through the outer margin.

title: Typography & color
summary: Create a readable hierarchy that survives real text and zoom.
points: Use a system font stack as a reliable starting point. Test fallback fonts as well as a preferred font.
rem relates to the root font size; em can depend on the current or inherited font size. Avoid assuming all users use the same default size.
A unitless line-height scales with each element’s font size. Keep body paragraphs comfortable to read.
Use a restrained color palette and check text/background contrast. Color alone must not communicate task status.
Allow text to wrap, expand, and zoom. Fixed-height text boxes can clip translated or enlarged content.
output: The heading grows with the viewport between its minimum and maximum. Body line spacing follows the body text size. The ch unit is based on the font’s zero glyph, not a guaranteed character count.
mistake: Light gray text on a pale card can look subtle but be hard to read. Check the actual color pair.
challenge: Give your planner a heading, body, and supporting-text scale. Test 200% zoom and convey “overdue” using words as well as color.

diagram.title: Typography & color
diagram.caption: Create a readable hierarchy that survives real text and zoom.

title: Flexbox layouts
summary: Arrange one dimension while letting content determine its size.
points: Put display: flex on the container. Its direct children become flex items.
flex-direction defines the main axis. justify-content works on that axis; align-items works on the cross axis.
Use gap between items and flex-wrap when items should flow to additional lines.
flex-grow, flex-shrink, and flex-basis describe how items share available space. min-width can still constrain shrinking.
Keep source order meaningful. Visual reordering does not reliably change reading or keyboard navigation order.
output: The toolbar can wrap when its contents no longer fit. An automatic end margin uses available space before the other controls.
mistake: justify-content: center is not always horizontal centering: the main axis changes with flex-direction.
challenge: Build a wrapping planner toolbar with a title and navigation links. Test with a long title and preserve the source order.

diagram.title: Flexbox layouts
diagram.caption: Arrange one dimension while letting content determine its size.

title: Grid layouts
summary: Use rows and columns to give a page a clear structure.
points: Put display: grid on the container, then define tracks with grid-template-columns or grid-template-rows.
fr shares remaining space. minmax(0, 1fr) allows a track to shrink below a content-based automatic minimum.
gap controls gutters without applying outer margins to every item.
repeat() reduces repetition. auto-fit and minmax() can create adaptable card columns.
Grid placement changes visual position, not the source reading order. Keep headings and controls logically ordered.
output: Two tracks share the available width equally after the gap. This snippet is for a wide layout; add the responsive rule from the next chapter for small screens.
mistake: A two-column layout at every width may squeeze content. Grid does not automatically make a page usable on a phone.
challenge: Arrange planner cards in a grid. Compare 1fr with minmax(0, 1fr) using an unbroken long title.

diagram.title: Grid layouts
diagram.caption: Use rows and columns to give a page a clear structure.

title: Responsive design
summary: Start with small screens and add space when the content needs it.
points: Include the viewport meta tag in HTML so mobile browsers use the device width for layout.
Write a simple base layout first. Use min-width media queries to enhance it at wider viewport sizes.
Choose breakpoints because content needs more space, not because one particular phone model exists.
Images usually need max-width: 100% and height: auto. Wide tables may need their own scroll container.
Check narrow widths, long content, zoom, and orientation. Do not hide essential content just to make a screenshot fit.
output: Cards stack by default and use two columns from the breakpoint upward. The stylesheet does not need to identify a device model.
mistake: Fixed widths and hidden overflow can conceal problems instead of making content responsive.
challenge: Test your planner at 320px, 768px, and a wide desktop. Add a long task title, zoom to 200%, and fix any clipped controls.

diagram.title: Responsive design
diagram.caption: Start with small screens and add space when the content needs it.

title: Focus & motion
summary: Make interaction understandable for keyboards and motion preferences.
points: Use :focus-visible to give keyboard navigation a clear visual indicator. Do not remove focus outlines without an equivalent replacement.
Pair hover feedback with keyboard-visible feedback. Touch devices may not have a persistent hover state.
Native disabled controls and visual disabled styling have different responsibilities. A gray color alone does not disable an action.
Limit transition properties and durations to what helps the interaction. Avoid distracting motion on essential controls.
Use prefers-reduced-motion to reduce nonessential transitions or animations. A preference query does not replace thoughtful defaults.
output: Focused links and buttons have a clear outline. People requesting reduced motion do not get this card transition.
mistake: A CSS class named disabled does not prevent clicks or form submission. Use native semantics and appropriate behavior.
challenge: Navigate every planner control with Tab and Shift+Tab. Turn on reduced motion in your OS and check that nonessential movement is removed.

diagram.caption: Make interaction understandable for keyboards and motion preferences.

title: Custom properties
summary: Name repeated decisions so a small theme stays consistent.
points: Custom properties start with -- and are read with var(). They participate in the cascade and normally inherit.
Define shared values on :root and override them within a component when that component needs a variation.
Use semantic names such as --surface or --accent to communicate intent. A token is a design decision, not only a shortcut.
var(--name, fallback) supplies a fallback when the custom property is unavailable or invalid as a variable. It is not a general type checker.
Organize styles into base rules, layout, components, and states. Keep dependencies easy to inspect.

rows: Change a value for a subtree

output: Cards share spacing and use the pink accent unless a local override supplies the calmer accent. The component rule stays the same.
mistake: A variable containing a value unsuitable for a property can invalidate that declaration; a fallback does not repair every bad value.
challenge: Extract repeated planner colors and spacing into custom properties. Change one token and inspect all affected components.

title: Style your student planner
summary: Combine readable design, responsive layout, and a practical self-review.
points: Keep the HTML course’s semantic structure. Add a linked stylesheet and a small palette, spacing scale, and typography hierarchy.
Use Flexbox for a toolbar and Grid for cards. Start with one column, then add wider arrangements when there is room.
Keep schedule tables inside a labelled region that can scroll locally when needed. Do not make the entire page overflow.
Review keyboard focus, meaningful source order, long task titles, and reduced-motion preferences.
Record before/after screenshots and meaningful Git commits. Explain two layout decisions in your README.
This project is static. A polished form is not a working task-saving feature; describe that limitation clearly.
output: The supplied starter gives you a working base and labelled exercises. Extend your earlier multi-page planner or start here; the checklist is self-assessed.
mistake: A high quiz score does not demonstrate a responsive project. Test the actual pages and explain your choices.
challenge: Complete the starter checklist, compare three viewport sizes, and write down one issue found with the keyboard and how you fixed it.
